title: The Neonatal Red-Cell Compartment as an Overlooked Glucose Sink: A Dual-Axis Hypothesis Linking Developmental Erythrocyte Biology to Neonatal Hypoglycaemia
content: Neonatal hypoglycaemia is among the most common metabolic disturbances of the newborn period, yet its pathophysiology is still framed almost entirely around hepatic glucose production, hyperinsulinism, and limited substrate reserves. A parallel literature—classical observations that neonatal polycythaemia and infants of diabetic mothers carry an elevated hypoglycaemia risk—has long been attributed vaguely to "increased glucose consumption by the red-cell mass," but without a molecular framework. The 2026 demonstration by Martí-Mateos and colleagues that hypoxia converts the adult red blood cell (RBC) into a quantitatively significant, GLUT1-driven glucose sink provides, for the first time, a candidate mechanism. Here we ask whether the developing red cell—forged in the physiological hypoxia of intrauterine life ("Everest in utero")—constitutes an analogous, developmentally programmed glucose sink, and whether this contributes to neonatal glucose lability. We deliberately separate two axes of the hypothesis and rate their evidence honestly. Axis I (per-mass, well-anchored clinically): the sheer size of the neonatal red-cell compartment—physiologically high haematocrit, amplified in polycythaemia and in infants of diabetic mothers—represents an under-quantified glucose-consuming pool; maternal and neonatal RBC indices are statistically associated with neonatal hypoglycaemia. Axis II (per-cell, currently unproven and partly counter-indicated): whether the individual fetal/neonatal red cell is intrinsically more "glucose-hungry" than the adult cell. We show that human data complicate the naïve version of Axis II: erythrocyte GLUT1 is already near-maximal on both neonatal and adult human RBCs, the low-oxygen activation of glycolysis is blunted rather than enhanced in newborn cells, and cord-blood RBC ATP is lower than adult. We argue these tensions do not refute the hypothesis but sharpen it: the fetal red cell occupies a distinct metabolic-oxygen coordinate (high oxygen affinity achieved through haemoglobin-F's insensitivity to 2,3-diphosphoglycerate rather than through a right-shifting glycolytic surge), and birth is a hyperoxic transition that triggers physiological neocytolysis. We propose a falsifiable, dual-axis research programme, situate the framework within a broader red-cell phenotype classification, and outline implications for neonatal glucose monitoring and for the interpretation of glycated haemoglobin in infancy.
